newsitem.title: USA: US jobless jump seen to mean labor mkt not heating.
newsitem.headline: US jobless jump seen to mean labor mkt not heating.

text.p: A rise in new jobless claims over the last two weeks may mean that the labor market, while still strong, is leveling, economists said.
"We're at a weekly claims level that we haven't seen since January," said Sandy Batten, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A.
The Labor Department reported on Thursday that new claims for state unemployment insurance jumped to 332,000 in the week ended April 12, up from a revised 324,000 new claims in the previous week.
The latest reading was higher than economists had estimated, according to a Reuters poll where the average forecast was for 317,000 new claims.
Claims for the week ended April 5 were revised up to 324,000 from the 318,000 new claims originally reported.

William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, said some work stoppages in the automotive industry could have biased the claims numbers upward.
"It's possible that some of these claims come from work interruptions in the automotive industry," he said.

But Sullivan said there was "no doubt that you get the sense that the decline in the level of new jobless claims filed has come to a halt. The data suggest that the momentum in the labor force may be leveling out."
Bond prices rose after the jobless claims data were released. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond climbed as much as 12/32 after the news, before trimming a third of that gain.

"Any kind of news that tells the bond market that the economy is not heating up anymore is positive for the bond market, especially after yesterday's (March industrial) production numbers were a little scary," said Batten.
Factory output rose 0.9 percent last month, surpassing economists expectations for a 0.6-percent increase.

John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust, said both the jobless claims data and the February U.S. trade figures released on Thursday morning were "modestly favorable for the (bond) market."

But Williams said that while new jobless claims have "edged up slightly, they remain at extremely low levels and indicate an extremely tight labor market that is likely to generate some upward pressure on employment costs."

Williams said that for now, a strong consumer would keep Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth high and that as a consequence, the Federal Reserve, "being somewhat forward-looking, will remain in a tightening mode until growth slows to a more sustainable pace."
